Chapter 36

Comments

The feature that deliberately does not use the CRDT, and the form instance per thread that stops one failure from decorating every thread.

By the end of this chapter

Know when a collaborative feature should be rows in a table instead.

When not to reach for the CRDT you just built

A comment is an event with an author and a time, not a value two people edit into a merged state. "We both replied at once" wants both replies — which is two rows, not a register with a winner. Building it on the document would mean inventing an append-only list inside a structure designed for mergeable values, to get behaviour a table gives you for nothing. Keeping comments out also means a commenter can be given comment rights without being handed write access to the board at all, which is the entire reason that role exists.

One query, assembled in memory. The alternative is a query for roots and one per root’s replies, which on a board with forty threads is forty-one round trips to answer a question the database could answer once. Threads are one level deep by design, so the assembly is a single pass.

A form() rather than a command(), for the reason from chapter 31 — it works without JavaScript — and for a second reason specific to this shape: postComment.for(threadId) gives every reply box its own instance from one definition. The parentId check in the middle is the subject of a section of its own, below.

$derived, not a plain const. threads(boardId) called once captures whichever board was open when the component mounted. Deriving it means navigating to another board re-runs the query — and, less obviously, it is what makes the compiler stop warning that the reference only captures the initial value, which is a warning worth listening to rather than silencing. It is the same reason chapter 30’s board page derives openBoard(params.board).

One definition, independent state

Spread the bare postComment into the loop and every thread shares one instance: a failed reply in one thread puts its error message under all of them, and the pending spinner appears on every button at once. .for(id) is the fix and it is four characters.

{const reply = $derived(…)} is a declaration tag, from chapter 30, and here its *scope* is the part worth seeing. A declaration tag’s name is visible to its siblings and to their children — in the documentation’s words, to “everything in the same lexical scope” — so reply reaches the whole <article> and nothing outside this {#each}. The legacy {@const} had to sit directly inside a block; a declaration tag can go anywhere in markup.

The check and the write name the same board

Resolving a thread is a command. Read it for what the where clause says, because the first version of it had a hole in exactly that line.

The question the check answered

requireAccess(board, who.id, 'commenter') answers a precise question: may this person comment on the board *the caller named*? The caller also names the thread, by id — and a row id says nothing about which board the row is on. The first version updated where(and(eq(comment.id, id), isNull(comment.parentId))): the right thread, on any board at all. Everybody who signs up owns a workspace and can make a board in it, so every viewer in the app was one devtools edit away from resolving threads on boards they can only look at: press Resolve, and change the boardId in the request to a board of their own. The check passed, for the board it was asked about. The write happened somewhere else.

The fix is one condition — eq(comment.boardId, board) — and the rule it stands for is worth more than the line: the access check and the row lookup must name the same board. A check that proves something about one id, followed by a write that matches on another, is not a check. And when nothing matches, the answer is 404, the same for “no such comment” as for “not on this board”, so a thread id is no more of an oracle than a board id was in chapter 18.

The same shape turns up wherever a remote function takes the id of a row *inside* a board. postComment takes a parentId, and looks it up with the board before it writes a reply to it — above. forgetCheckpoint deletes a checkpoint by id:

The test forges the request the way an attacker would: it presses the real button and rewrites the command’s argument on the way out with Playwright’s page.route. The seed gives the viewer a workspace and a board of their own for exactly this, because every account made through the sign-up form has one — a fixture in which the viewer is *only* a viewer is a fixture in which this bug cannot be seen.

When the server says no

A viewer can see the comment box, the Reply boxes and the Resolve button. Hiding them would be a courtesy, and courtesies get forgotten; what actually stops a viewer is requireAccess(…, 'commenter') in postComment and resolveThread, which answers 403 — about the board the write is really scoped to, now. The interface’s job is to say so, in the server’s words, next to the thing that was refused.

Why body.message

A command the server refuses rejects with an HttpError — { status, body } — and an HttpError is not an Error, so thrown.message is undefined and the obvious line shows nothing at all. The first version did not even get that far: it had no catch, the rejection went nowhere, and pressing the button did nothing anybody could see. isHttpError(thrown) narrows the type, body.message is the server’s sentence, and anything that is not an HttpError — a request that never got an answer — gets the generic line.

The two forms go through send, by way of enhance:

Why enhance

A form spread without enhance handles its own failures, and the documentation says how: “if an error occurs during submission, the nearest +error.svelte page will be rendered.” For this panel the nearest one is the root error page — the board page resets its layout with @, and no layout in between has one — so a viewer who typed a comment and pressed Post lost the whole editor to find out they may not post. enhance hands the submission to the component: form.submit() rejects with the same HttpError a command does, and send turns it into a line under the form, with the comment still in the box. The documentation also says what enhance takes away — “the <form> is not automatically reset — you must call form.element.reset()” — which is why send clears the box only once submit() reports success.

{uid}-new rather than id="new-comment". A fixed id is unique until the component is rendered twice — two panels, a test that mounts two — and then two labels point at one textarea. $props.id() “generates an ID that is unique to the current component instance”, the same on the server and after hydration, and the documentation’s example is exactly this: linking a <label for> to its control.

The list, awaited where it is shown

This is the idiom, and it is the same one the board page and the board list use: the query awaited in this component’s own markup, inside its own <svelte:boundary>, with declaration tags naming what is derived from it. The wait is this boundary’s pending snippet, a failure is its failed snippet, and the rest of the editor never notices either. open and resolved are $derived declaration tags, so a refresh after a post or a resolve re-runs the split and nothing else.

Why not .current

A query also has current, loading and error, and the documentation offers them plainly as the second choice: “while using await is recommended, as an alternative the query also has loading, error and current properties.” This panel used them for a while, on the theory that an await would suspend the whole component. That is true of an await in the *script*; one in the markup suspends only its boundary. What the properties cost is every branch written by hand — loading, error, empty — and nothing to stop a fallback showing at the wrong moment. The first version showed “No comments yet” over a query that had failed: a fallback that always won, and the one line on the panel that was confidently wrong. Reach for .current when you want the rest of a component to render without waiting and are prepared to handle undefined and .error yourself.

Checkpoint

  • A colleague’s comment appears without a refresh.
  • A failed reply shows its error under one thread only.
  • A viewer who presses Resolve or Post is told why not, in the server’s words, and keeps the board.
  • A request that names one board and a thread on another is answered 404, not obeyed.
  • A commenter can comment and cannot move a box.
